newsitem.title: USA: NSC reviews White House access, briefing procedures.
newsitem.headline: NSC reviews White House access, briefing procedures.

text.p: National Security Adviser Samuel "Sandy" Berger is studying new procedures on screening foreign citizens who visit the White House, presidential spokesman Mike McCurry said on Thursday.

McCurry also said Berger was looking at ways to ensure key information gets to senior officials because of an embarassing 1996 incident when two National Security Council (NSC) intelligence specialists failed to brief their superiors about a suspected Chinese effort to buy U.S. political influence.
China has strongly denied the allegations.
"Sandy Berger is looking at procedures for making sure that information that needs to be briefed up the chain of command at the NSC absolutely for certain gets briefed up," McCurry told reporters.
The spokesman also said Berger was "working with the White House legal counsel about steps that they would take ... to monitor foreigners who come here to the White House for any purpose."
Earlier this year the White House said two NSC officials received a briefing from Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) officials but failed to tell their superiors about it.
The White House initially said the two were instructed by the FBI not to pass along the information, prompting a startling public denial from the law enforcement agency.
Eventually both sides said there appeared to have been a misunderstanding on the matter, but it left questions about whether the president gets all the information he may need.

Clinton has come under intense scrutiny since the 1996 election for the fund-raising practices of his Democratic Party, which has returned nearly $3 million in donations that it deemed questionable, much of it from Asian sources.

In one incident, Clinton's Arkansas friend Charlie Trie invited the head of a weapons trading firm owned by the Chinese government, Wang Jun, to a private White House coffee with Clinton. The incident led to questions about whether the Clinton administration kept close enough track of foreigners brought to the White House.

McCurry said Berger would consult former National Security Advisers Zbigniew Brzezinski and Brent Scowcroft on procedures under past adminstrations. He said Berger's recommendations, when finished, would go to the White House chief of staff.
